&l;p&g;&l;img class=&q;dam-image shutterstock size-large wp-image-1061172590&q; src=&q;https://specials-images.forbesimg.com/dam/imageserve/1061172590/960×0.jpg?fit=scale&q; data-height=&q;640&q; data-width=&q;960&q;&g; Shutterstock 
National Beer Day falls on April 7 and marks the day that beer was allowed to be legally manufactured and sold following a long, dry Prohibition. On March 22, 1933, President Franklin Roosevelt signed the Cullen&a;ndash;Harrison Act into law which moved the U.S. away from Prohibition by allowing the manufacture and sale of beer which was approximately 4% alcohol by volume (just a little less than the average today) and some wines. After he signed, Roosevelt reportedly &l;a href=&q;http://100days.blogs.nytimes.com/2009/01/16/how-fdr-made-the-presidency-matter/?_r=0&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;remarked to his aide&l;/a&g;, Louis Howe, &q;I think this would be a good time for a beer.&q; 
Prohibition would officially remain in place for a few more months, but the ability to drink beer and wine was worth cheering. Here are a few more facts about beer – and its close relationship to tax – to help you celebrate in 2018: 
1. Egypt was likely the first civilization to tax beer. Queen Cleopatra imposed a tax on beer in order, she claimed, to discourage public drunkenness, though it is believed that the tax was&a;nbsp;&l;a href=&q;http://www.beeradvocate.com/articles/629/&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;used&l;/a&g; to raise money to fund a war with Rome. 
2. Beer is the &l;a href=&q;http://news.gallup.com/poll/214229/beer-remains-preferred-alcoholic-beverage.aspx&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;most popular alcoholic beverage&l;/a&g; in the United States. According to a 2017 Gallup poll, 40% of Americans who drink alcohol say they prefer beer, down a few percentage points from last year. In 2016, the federal government collected &l;a href=&q;https://www.irs.gov/statistics/soi-tax-stats-excise-tax-statistics&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;$3.6 billion&l;/a&g; in excise taxes on domestic and imported beer alone. 
3. In 1695, Great Britain raised taxes on beer, making gin the cheapest beverage in England. Gin was taxed at 2d (about 2 pennies) per gallon, while beer was taxed at 4 shillings 9d (about 57 pennies) per gallon. The &l;a href=&q;http://www.politics.co.uk/reference/alcohol-duties&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;difference in price&l;/a&g; is considered the root of a serious drinking problem in the country in the 18th century, especially among the poor. 
4. In the United States, taxes on the production, distribution, and sale typically eat up 40% of the retail price of beer. That amount includes all taxes imposed on beer. In previous years, the federal excise tax was about &l;a href=&q;http://www.cspinet.org/booze/taxguide/FedBeerTax_M_F.htm&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;5 cents per drink&l;/a&g;&a;nbsp;(the nickel comes from the assumption that the average beer has an alcohol content of 4.5%). 
5. If you thought &l;a href=&q;http://www.forbes.com/sites/kellyphillipserb/2017/12/15/its-beginning-to-look-a-lot-like-tax-reform-heres-whats-in-the-final-version/&q;&g;tax reform&l;/a&g; only lowered income taxes, you&s;d be mistaken. The &l;a href=&q;https://www.forbes.com/sites/peterjreilly/2017/12/19/tax-cuts-and-jobs-act-whiskey-for-my-men-beer-for-my-horses/#6585de7c7d82&q;&g;new law&l;/a&g; reduced the federal excise tax on beer according to output. Those rates were &l;a href=&q;http://www.beerinstitute.org/beer-policy/legislative-policy/excise-tax/&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;reduced&l;/a&g; to $3.50 per barrel on the first 60,000 barrels for domestic brewers producing fewer than 2 million barrels annually and $16 per barrel on the first 6 million barrels for all other brewers and all beer importers; the excise tax remains at $18 per barrel rate for&a;nbsp;those producing over 6 million. If those rates sound familiar, they closely mirror previously proposed legislation, including &l;a href=&q;https://www.forbes.com/sites/kellyphillipserb/2013/05/11/us-reps-to-house-beer-me/#5d67e93e1fd3&q;&g;the BEER Act&l;/a&g;&a;nbsp;of 2013. There is one downside: Under tax reform, most corporate changes under tax reform are permanent and most individual changes are effective through 2025,&a;nbsp;the changes&a;nbsp;affecting the beer market will expire in 2020. 
6. German beers are often labeled &q;Gebraut nach dem Bayerischen Reinheitsgebot von 1516&q; which translates roughly to &q;brewed according to the &l;a href=&q;http://brewery.org/library/ReinHeit.html&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;Bavarian Purity Law of 1516&l;/a&g;.&q; The law originally limited the ingredients which can be used to make beer in Germany (barley malt, hops, yeast, and water) and allowed the government to tax beer. The Reinheitsgebot became an official part of the German tax code in 1919 but was largely gutted when Germany became part of the European Union. 
7. To help pay for the Civil War, Congress imposed an excise tax on beer. The Revenue Act of 1862, signed into law by President Lincoln, &l;a href=&q;http://memory.loc.gov/cgi-bin/ampage&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;included a tax&l;/a&g; on &q;all beer, lager beer, ale, porter, and other similar fermented liquors, by whatever name such liquors may be called.&q; It may not be popular but taxing beer wasn&s;t a bad idea from an economic standpoint, as it generates billions in revenue each year. 
&l;!–donotpaginate–&g; 
8. Arthur Guinness II – the father of Guinness stout – altered the family beer recipe to include unmalted roasted barley instead of black malt. The unmalted barley wasn&s;t subject to extra taxes (more on those &l;a href=&q;https://www.forbes.com/sites/kellyphillipserb/2016/03/17/you-can-thank-excise-taxes-for-guinness-stout/#3d2f0dba5bf7&q;&g;here&l;/a&g;) which made it affordable for the Guinness family – it also made the beer&s;s taste distinctive. By the end of the 19th century, Guinness was the &l;a href=&q;http://powersbrewery.com/porter-stout-history/&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;largest brewery&l;/a&g; in Europe. 
9.&a;nbsp;&l;a href=&q;http://www.beerinstitute.org/economic-impact/&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;According to the Beer Institute&l;/a&g;, last year, directly and indirectly, the beer industry employed&a;nbsp;nearly 2.23 million Americans, providing more than $103 billion in wages and benefits. The industry pays nearly $63 billion in business, personal and consumption taxes. 
10. In 1991, President George H.W. Bush signed a bill which raised taxes on luxuries such as furs, yachts, private jets, jewelry and expensive cars (despite the &q;no new taxes&q; pledge) – that same bill nearly doubled the tax on beer. Bush&a;nbsp;&l;a href=&q;http://articles.latimes.com/1992-01-31/business/fi-1159_1_luxury-tax&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;called for the repeal&l;/a&g; of the tax just two years later, and while most of the taxes included in the bill were eventually repealed, the tax on beer remained in place and is still there today. 
11. The most expensive state to buy a beer may be Tennessee where &l;a href=&q;https://www.salestaxhandbook.com/tennessee/alcohol&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;state excise taxes&l;/a&g; reach a whopping $1.29 per gallon, plus sales tax, making it the highest in the country. The cheapest state to buy a beer? Wyoming, where the&a;nbsp;excise tax is&a;nbsp;&l;a href=&q;https://www.salestaxhandbook.com/wyoming/alcohol&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;just $.02 per gallon&l;/a&g;. 
12. The oldest operating brewing company in the U.S. is D.G. Yuengling &a;amp; Son, owned by &l;a href=&q;http://www.forbes.com/profile/richard-yuengling-jr/&q;&g;Forbes billionaire Richard Yuengling, Jr.&l;/a&g; Yuengling (&q;Ying-ling&q; and not &q;Yoong-ling&q; or &q;Yang-ling&q;), based in Pottsville, Pennsylvania, is one of the country&s;s five largest beer companies with an estimated $550 million in annual revenue in 2015. The company&a;nbsp;added a new location in Florida&a;nbsp;and won&s;t promise to remain in Pennsylvania, blaming the &l;a href=&q;http://www.pennlive.com/midstate/index.ssf/2012/10/yuengling_new_brewery.html&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;state&s;s tax climate&l;/a&g; in 2012: &q;Pennsylvania is a great location. But it&a;rsquo;s not very business-friendly. You look for fair tax breaks, fair taxation. And the bottom line is more jobs. That&a;rsquo;s what it&a;rsquo;s all about.&q; 
13. &l;a href=&q;http://www.infogroup.com/about/news/bend-or-ranks-as-no-1-hidden-beer-gem-in-the-us&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;According to Infogroup&l;/a&g;, with 1.54 beer-related businesses per capita, Bend, Oregon is the most favorable U.S. city for beer lovers. Oregon boasts two cities on the list. It probably helps that Oregon has &l;a href=&q;https://www.oregon.gov/DOR/Pages/sales-tax.aspx&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;no state sales tax&l;/a&g; to boost prices. 
14. Sales of craft beer increased 8%, up to $26.0 billion, &l;a href=&q;https://www.brewersassociation.org/statistics/national-beer-sales-production-data/&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;according to the Brewers Association&l;/a&g;, and now account for more than 23% of the beer market. California leads the way,&a;nbsp;boasting&a;nbsp;2.2&a;nbsp;breweries per capita. You see how your state ranks &l;a href=&q;https://www.brewersassociation.org/statistics/by-state/&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;here&l;/a&g;. 
15. In addition to sales of beer, &q;beer tourism&q; is a real thing. Sites like &l;a href=&q;http://www.brewtrail.com/about/&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;BrewTrail.com&l;/a&g;&a;nbsp;help consumers plan road trips and vacations around visits to breweries, which bring additional&a;nbsp;&l;a href=&q;https://www.forbes.com/sites/kellyphillipserb/2014/07/07/the-real-cost-of-summer-vacation-dont-get-buried-in-taxes/#77d1a54e597a&q;&g;travel tax dollars&l;/a&g;. States and regions have gotten into the spirit, offering info on their own &q;ale trail&q; recommendations. One example? Just last week, my husband and I left our stamp on my hometown economy via the&a;nbsp;&l;a href=&q;http://wilmingtonaletrail.com/&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;Wilmington Ale Trail&l;/a&g;&a;nbsp;(one of our favorites&a;nbsp;was&a;nbsp;&l;a href=&q;http://www.flytrapbrewing.com/&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;Flytrap Brewing&l;/a&g;). 
16. Cenosillicaphobia is the fear of an empty beer glass. Okay, that&s;s not a tax fact, of course, just a fact. Don&s;t live in fear: go,&a;nbsp;get a beer.&l;/p&g; This entry was posted in Best Stocks on
